tweets.text:
Great post on FDEs. Everyone should read it if you’re interested in this job category. This is a job that is going to be around as long as AI keeps changing rapidly, which it inevitably will. 

People often wonder why isn’t this like just deploying other forms of technology in the past, like cloud. 

Because something like cloud adoption affected a fairly concentrated set of users (developers and IT), and generally didn’t require a fundamental change to the workflows of employees to get the benefits of the new service being delivered on the cloud. At best you went to one training session and you were done. 

With agents, the work to implement them is not only highly technical, but they directly impact the underlying workflows that people participate in. This means there’s a ton of technical work and change management that comes with it.

Further, the pace of change of cloud wasn’t nearly as quick, so there was a lot more time for best practices to propagate. Now, every model change means either something new can be done that wasn’t possible before, or some piece of scaffolding is now redundant or holding you back. 

This is why it’s commonly easier for a vendor or partner that’s seen the implementation hundreds or thousands of times help do the work, even with internal support from the customer.

So, this job isn’t going away any time soon, and will be a great path for a lot of technical talent, especially early career.

tweets.text:
EIGHT. 8️⃣ 

That's how many Ethereum Foundation departures have happened since February. And somehow, the institutional money is still piling in at the same time. $7.5B in tokenized treasuries. $1.4B money market fund. 66.8% RWA market share.

Ethereum is having the most contradictory week in recent memory.

→ David Hoffman's tweet ("was that just me selling the last of my ETH?") hit 880 Signal, the highest of any ETH tweet in seven days. More than any protocol announcement. More than any institutional news. Just a guy asking a question the whole community was already thinking.

→ Ryan Sean Adams announced the "first era of Bankless has concluded" in the same 24-hour window. The two biggest voices in Ethereum media stepping back simultaneously is not something people are willing to file under coincidence.

→ The institutional counter-narrative ran hard in parallel. Franklin Templeton's BENJI became the largest tokenized money market fund on Ethereum at $1.4B, up 50% in a month. Galaxy Digital launched a $125M ETH fund. ETH holds 66.8% TVL share of the entire RWA market. The fundamentals did not get the memo about the vibe shift.

→ Protocol-side kept moving too. EIP-7928 confirmed for the Glamsterdam hardfork. Ronin Network migrated to ETH L2. Community noise is running louder than foundation comms right now.

→ Sentiment is split and probably should be. DCinvestor: "the next cycle will be bigger than even I can imagine for ETH." jez: "thanks for everything eth, even if I don't own u anymore." Both things, true at the same time. The exits and the inflows arrived at the same party this week. Nobody's agreed on what that means yet.

One of the toughest parts of being a founder is putting your ideas into the world, seeing if anyone cares (usually they don't - or worse, are rooting against you), and then seeing if you can actually pull it off (usually way more setbacks along the way than you thought!).

You have to: 
(1) develop thick skin and find a way to ignore the haters 
(2) still take advice from people who have your best interests at heart
(3) have the wisdom to know the difference

Then move from one setback to the next with no loss of enthusiasm for longer than you thought. Be borderline delusional, get after it every day for a decade, and turn out to be right. Finally, when your tenth or hundredth approach to a problem doesn't work, just keep coming up with more ideas.

Had a great day at Base Batches yesterday, meeting founders building on @base and hearing about the latest onchain innovations. Shout out to all the founders!
